title: the Kama Sutra's ethics chapter (not the rest)
hook: a pigeon today, or a peacock tomorrow?
carry: the Kama Sutra's ethics chapter (not the rest)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kama Sutra's ethics chapter answered pleasure's critics: plant the barley, and watch for deer. Today, a second set of critics, from the other side.

The paycheck job that starts Monday, or the unpaid internship that might lead somewhere. A group chat will split down the middle on that one, and somebody always types: take the sure thing. In the Kama Sutra's opening, that voice has a name and a slogan. The Lokayatikas, thinkers who trust only what they can see, say a pigeon today is better than a peacock tomorrow. And a copper coin you're sure of beats a gold coin you're not.
screen: `THE SURE THING, OR THE MAYBE?` → `A PIGEON TODAY.` → `A PEACOCK TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: The book gives their case room, so hear it whole. Dharma promises its rewards later, somewhere no one has checked. Meanwhile it asks you to give things up now. Why trade something real for a rumor? A pigeon in the hand can feed you tonight. That's a serious view, and the chapter states it in its own sharp words. A book on pleasure might be expected to cheer. It doesn't. Vatsyayana answers that the teaching on dharma comes from scripture, and he treats it as trustworthy, not as a guess. Then he goes back to the field. A farmer puts seed in the ground for a crop he hasn't seen. Nobody calls that foolish. Acting now for a good you can't yet see is something people do every planting season. So the two voices stand side by side. One says: only what's in your hand is real. The other says: so is a seed in the ground. And notice who stands where. The book of pleasure is the one defending the reward that can't be seen yet.
screen: `THE LOKAYATIKAS: TAKE THE SURE THING.` · `VATSYAYANA: DHARMA RESTS ON SCRIPTURE.` · `A FARMER SOWS FOR AN UNSEEN CROP.` · then, large: `A SEED IN THE GROUND IS REAL TOO.`

segments.voice: Pick one choice in front of you where the sure thing pulls against the slow one. Say the sure thing's best case out loud, quietly, in one sentence, as if you believed it. Then say the slow one's best case the same way, and sit with both sentences in the air, choosing nothing yet.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: here, the Lokayatikas' pigeon in the hand, answered by a farmer's seed.

fork.setup: two cousins argue over graduation money: spend it now, or save it for later. give the 'spend it now' side its best case, in the Lokayatikas' words.

fork.reveal: the Lokayatikas trust what's in hand: a pigeon today over a peacock tomorrow. Vatsyayana's answer is the farmer, who sows for a crop he can't see yet.

chat.meaning: The Lokayatikas trust only what's in hand; Vatsyayana answers that a farmer sows for an unseen crop. The chapter lets both be real before choosing.
